note: Drafted by the chat assistant 11-05 for the owner's review (D154 P2): the first 'match' and 'order' items for the daily question and Play. Nothing is live until approved. For match: 'answer[i]' is the index in 'right' that matches 'left[i]'. For order: 'answer' lists the indices of 'steps' in the correct order.

items.stem: Match each HTTP status code to the situation it describes.
right: The client has hit its rate limit
A new order was stored
The request has no valid credentials
The request body failed validation
why: 201 tells the client the resource now exists, usually with its location.
400 means the request itself is wrong, so retrying it unchanged won't help.
401 means 'who are you?': sign in first. (403 means 'I know who you are, and no'.)
429 asks the client to slow down, ideally with a Retry-After header.

items.stem: Match each data structure to the job it does best.
right: Always take the most urgent task next
Suggest words as someone types a prefix
Process print jobs in the order they arrived
Look up a user by id in constant time on average
why: Hashing the key jumps straight to the right bucket, so lookups don't scan.
First in, first out keeps the arrival order.
A heap keeps the highest-priority item on top, with cheap inserts and removals.
Each prefix is a path in the tree, so every word starting with it sits below one node.

items.stem: Match each join to the result it gives, joining orders to customers (or sizes to colours).
right: Every order and every customer, matched where possible
Only orders that have a matching customer
Every order, with customer details where they exist
Every combination of size and colour
why: Inner keeps only rows that match on both sides.
Left keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with nulls when there's no match.
Full outer keeps everything from both sides, matched where it can.
Cross pairs every row with every row: useful for combinations, dangerous by accident.

items.stem: Match each Kubernetes object to what it's for.
right: Hold non-secret settings the pods read at start-up
Route outside HTTP traffic by host or path to services
Keep three copies of the app running and roll out new versions
Give the pods one stable address inside the cluster
why: A Deployment manages the pods' desired count and rolling updates.
Pods come and go; a Service gives them one name and spreads traffic across them.
An Ingress is the front door for HTTP traffic from outside the cluster.
Settings live outside the image, so the same build runs in every environment. Secrets go in a Secret, not here.

items.stem: Match each attack to its main defence.
right: Parameterised queries
Multi-factor sign-in and rate-limited logins
Encoding output, plus a Content Security Policy
SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens
why: Parameters keep data separate from the query, so input can't change it.
Encoding stops injected markup running, and a CSP limits what can run at all.
The browser won't send the session cookie from another site, and the token proves the request came from your page.
Leaked passwords from other sites stop working on their own, and rate limits slow the guessing.

items.stem: Match each metric to the question it answers.
right: On average, how far off are our price predictions?
How slow are the slowest 5% of predictions?
Of all the real fraud, how much did we catch?
Of the transactions we flagged, how many were really fraud?
why: Precision is about the flags you raised: how many were right.
Recall is about the cases out there: how many you found.
MAE is the average size of the error, in the target's own units.
The 95th percentile shows the slow tail that averages hide.

items.stem: You type a web address and press Enter. Put the steps in the order they happen.
steps: Agree on encryption (the TLS handshake)
Look up the server's IP address (DNS)
Show the response in the browser
Open a TCP connection to the server
Send the HTTP request
items.why: Name to address, then a connection, then encryption on that connection, then the request, then the page. (Newer HTTP/3 merges the connection and encryption steps, but the order of ideas is the same.)

items.stem: Put the steps of a blue-green deployment in order.
steps: Switch traffic to the new version
Run health checks and smoke tests on the new version
Deploy the new version alongside the old one
Watch error rates and latency
Retire the old version once the new one is stable
items.why: The old version keeps serving until the new one has proved healthy; switching is instant, and keeping the old one around until things settle means a rollback is one switch back.

items.stem: Put the steps of handling a security incident in order.
steps: Review: a blameless postmortem with fixes
Contain it: isolate the affected systems
Detect and confirm the incident
Recover: restore systems and watch them closely
Remove the cause: close the attacker's way in
items.why: Confirm before acting, contain before cleaning (so it can't spread while you work), remove the cause before restoring (or it comes straight back), then learn from it.

items.stem: You need to rename a column in a live database without downtime. Put the steps in order.
steps: Stop writing the old column, then drop it
Copy existing values into the new column
Write to both the old and new columns
Switch reads to the new column
Add the new column
items.why: This is the expand-and-contract pattern: at every step, both the old and new code keep working, so you can deploy each step separately and stop or roll back at any point.

items.stem: Put the steps of shipping a feature through code review in order.
steps: Commit your changes with their tests
Create a branch from main
Address the review comments
Open a pull request
Merge once CI passes
items.why: A branch keeps main clean, tests travel with the change, review comes before merge, and the merge waits for green CI.

items.stem: Put the steps of building and shipping a model in order.
steps: Ship behind a shadow test or A/B test, and monitor
Train and tune on the training data
Evaluate once on the held-out test set
Choose the metric and a simple baseline
Split the data (by time if the data is time-based)
items.why: Decide what good means first, keep a clean test set before you train, touch the test set once at the end, and prove it in production before it replaces anything.
